title: Should You Risk the Parking Ticket?
objective: After this level you can use expected value to compare two everyday choices, like paying for parking or risking a fine.
summary: Compare a sure cost with the expected cost of a gamble. With a $4 meter, a $50 fine and a 1 in 5 chance of a ticket, skipping costs $10 on average. The choices break even at a chance of 8 in 100.

cards.headline: The meter costs $4. The fine is $50. Pay, or take your chances?
cards.body: Nobody calls it a bet, but it is one. Let's put made-up round numbers on it and let expected value decide.

cards.headline: The cost of skipping, on average
cards.body: Suppose 1 time in 5 you'd get a ticket. Skipping then costs $50 × 1/5, or $10 on average, against a sure $4 at the meter. Paying saves you $6 a visit on average. Even if tickets came only 1 time in 10, skipping would cost $5 on average: still more than the meter.

cards.headline: Find the break-even point
cards.body: Where would the choice flip? When the expected fine equals the meter: the chance times $50 equals $4. That happens at a chance of 4 in 50, or 8 in 100. Unless tickets were rarer than that, the meter is the better deal. Finding the break-even chance works for any either-or choice: it tells you how likely the bad outcome must be before the gamble stops paying.

cards.fact: Expected value counts only what you put into it.
cards.context: The sum above includes the fine and nothing else. Any cost you leave out of the calculation, like lost time or a ruined afternoon, can't show up in the answer. So a neat average can make a gamble look cheaper than it feels. Level 35's risk-averse buyer knew that already.

cards.headline: The parking bet: decided
learned: Skipping costs chance × fine on average
The average counts only what you put in
